==English==

===Etymology===
Synchronically equivalent to {{suffix|en|tight|en|id2=inchoative}}, but actually derived from {{inh|en|enm|tighten}}, from {{inh|en|ang|tyhtan}}, thus originally unrelated to {{m|en|tight}} (Old English {{m|ang|*þiht}}).

===Pronunciation===
* {{IPA|en|/ˈtaɪ.tən/|[ˈtʰaɪ̯tn̩]|[ˈtʰaɪ̯ʔn̩]}}
** {{audio|en|LL-Q1860 (eng)-Vealhurl-tighten.wav|a=Southern England}}
* {{rhymes|en|aɪtən|s=2}}
* {{homophones|en|titan|Titan}}

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To make [[tight]]er.
#: {{syn|en|cinch}}
#: {{ux|en|Please '''tighten''' that screw a quarter-turn.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1760|author=w:Francis Fawkes|title=Works of Anacreon, Sappho, Bion, Moschus, and Musæus translated into English by a gentleman of Cambridge
|passage=Just where I please, with '''tighten;d''' rein / I'll urge thee round the dusty plain.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To become tighter.
#: {{ux|en|That joint is '''tightening''' as the wood dries.}}
# {{lb|en|economics}} To make money harder to borrow or obtain.
#: {{ux|en|If the government doesn't '''tighten''' the money supply, inflation is certain to be harsh.}}
# {{lb|en|economics}} To raise short-term interest rates.
#: {{ux|en|The Fed is expected to '''tighten''' by a quarter-point.}}

====Antonyms====
* {{antsense|make tighter}} {{l|en|loosen}}
